newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - UK managers raise cash, shun stocks - survey.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK managers raise cash, shun stocks - survey.

text.p: British fund managers raised their cash levels for the first time in a year in July amid expectations global stock markets will fall in the next three months, a survey showed on Monday.

Conducted by Gallup for investment bank Merrill Lynch between August 4 and August 6, a day before the Bank of England (BoE) raised official interest rates to 7.0 percent from 6.75 percent, the survey also revealed that fund managers continued to favour gilts over British stocks, which were reached historic levels last week.
Gallup asked 68 leading British institutions controlling funds of 1.093 trillion pounds ($1.7 trillion) about their outlook for the economy and their asset allocation plans.
Only a quarter of fund managers said they expected British economic activity to be stronger a year from now, down from 32 percent last month.
The growing conviction that the British economy would cool down may explain why managers were shifting their portfolios into gilts and away from British stocks, Merrill said.
Respondents were keen sellers of UK equities, with sellers outnumbering buyers by 12 percent, while buyers of gilts outnumbered sellers by 22 percent, the survey said.
"The move to gilts is not a bad switch to make, but we prefer switching into cash, Merrill Lynch global strategist Trevor Greetham said in a telephone interview.

"UK fund managers already have piles of cash, and they're gradually building it up even more, he said. "We've been recommending pension funds raise cash to 7.5 percent, two percent above the average. I have a hunch that if we continue to see this blood bath in Treasuries, people will move wholeheartedly into cash."
Respondents said they expected British base rates to rise to 7.5 percent a year from 7.0 percent now.

They expected British corporate earnings and dividends to slow, yet were less bullish about sterling. Only 11 percent of the fund managers were expecting a further appreciation in the currency over the next 12 months, down from 33 percent last month.

Greetham said he expects next month's survey to reflect even less optimism about sterling among fund managers in the wake of the central bank's most recent move to tighten and comment that the current rate is now consistent with its inflation target.

Fund managers were positive only on stock markets in continental Europe, where corporations can benefit from relatively weak domestic currencies, Greetham noted. Additionally, economies in continental Europe are not as far along and therefore, are unlikely to see rates rise soon, he said.
The survey showed that 21 percent of fund managers were positive three months out on continental European stocks, up from 16 percent in the last survey.
Respondents were most bearish on Pacific Basin equities. Fifteen percent were forecasting a drop in those markets, up from seven percent in the previous month.
The percentage of fund managers who were negative about U.S. stocks fell to nine percent from 27 percent in the previous survey.

Greetham said he expects the U.S. Federal Reserve to tighten credit soon, which is likely to halt the historic seven-year bull run in global stock markets. --London Newsroom +44 171 542 5106 ($ = 0.630 British Pounds)
